topic: What if you had an iPhone 100 years ago?

script.text: At first, it's amazing. You walk into a jazz club and play a song from a hundred years in the future. The band stops. Then they try to copy it. By midnight, the whole room is dancing to a beat that doesn't exist yet.
The bandleader offers to buy the song. You tell him it's not yours to sell. Not for another eighty years.

A kid called Mo starts following you everywhere. You show him a video. Moving pictures, with sound. He doesn't blink for a whole minute. Movies here don't talk. The first feature film with spoken scenes won't come out until October 1927. That's real.
You show him a photo of a city at night. Towers of glass, lit up like Christmas. Mo whispers, 'Is that heaven?' You say, 'No. It's Tuesday.'
You take a selfie with a crowd of strangers. Flash. The whole street gasps. The next morning, a newspaper prints a drawing of you: The Boy With the Lightning Box.
Then you start making money. In 1926, a computer isn't a machine. It's a person with a pencil, paid to do math all day. You race ten of them with your calculator. You win before lunch.
You record a banker saying hello, and play it back. He pays you twenty dollars just to hear his own voice again.

Mo's mom runs a boarding house, and she gives you a room. His little sister, Ellie, makes you show her the flashlight every single night. 'Make the star again.' You're the most interesting person in New York.
Then you look at the corner of the screen. Sixty-two percent.

science.claim: The first feature film with spoken scenes won't come out until October 1927.
science.working: The Jazz Singer, the first feature presented as a talkie (with limited synchronized dialogue sequences), premiered 6 October 1927. Don Juan (1926) had synchronized music and effects but no dialogue.

science.claim: In 1926, a 'computer' was a person paid to do calculations.
science.working: Until electronic computers took over in the late 1940s and 1950s, 'computer' was a job title for people who did calculations by hand.
